content.title: Michigan’s Yaxel Lendeborg Credits His Mother With Turning His Life Around
content.text: 4 min readYaxel Lendeborg had a decision to make in the spring of 2025: Enter the NBA draft as a projected first-round pick, or return to college for one more season. He chose Michigan, which reportedly offered $3 million in NIL compensation. At the same time, he reportedly turned down a much higher offer from Kentucky, reportedly in the range of $7 million to $9 million. The gamble on one more college season proved well-founded as Michigan made it to the 2026 NCAA Men’s Final Four, and he went on to become a consensus All-American and the Big Ten Player of the Year with the Wolverines.Born September 30, 2002, in Puerto Rico, Yaxel moved to Ohio with his family at age two before settling in New Jersey at age eight. He began his college career at Arizona Western before transferring to University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB) in 2023. In April 2025, he transferred again to Michigan. He entered the 2025 NBA draft process shortly after, was projected as a late first-round or early second-round pick—a range that carried a potential four-year rookie contract worth around $14 million—before withdrawing in May.Michael Reaves//Getty ImagesYaxel with his parents, Okary (left) and Yissel (right) after the Elite Eight round of the 2026 NCAA Men’s Basketball Tournament on March 29.In a recent essay for The Players’ Tribune, titled “How My Mom Saved My Life,” Yaxel wrote about how his mother’s efforts especially guided him on the long and hard but ultimately successful path to Ann Arbor, Michigan.Advertisement - Continue Reading Below“Because there were literally hundreds of times over the years when my mom could’ve given up on me. Times when, honestly, she would’ve had every right to give up on me,” Yaxel wrote. “But she never did. And now here I am. Here we are. And now that we’re here??? Man…I just want to be the kind of person who was worth not giving up on. I just want to be the player she always believed in me to become.”Below, get to know Yaxel’s parents, Yissel Raposo and Okary Lendeborg.Meet Yaxel’s dad, Okary Lendeborg:Yaxel's father, Pedro, played basketball for the Dominican Republic national team. A job opportunity eventually brought the family from Puerto Rico to Pennsauken Township, New Jersey, just across the river from Philadelphia. But Okary has said in interviews that Yaxel and his siblings spent much of their time with their mother while he was working. “I would work and she would be stuck with him and every day they were together,” Okary told USA Today through a translator about Yaxel and his mother. “That just became his role model.”Meet Yaxel’s mom, Yissel Raposo:Aaron J. Thornton//Getty ImagesYissel Raposo, wearing Yaxel’s No. 23 Michigan jersey, during the Sweet Sixteen round on March 27.Advertisement - Continue Reading BelowYissel Raposo, Yaxel’s mother, played volleyball for both the Dominican Republic national team and the American University of Puerto Rico. She is also the person that Yaxel credits as most responsible for turning his life around.Growing up, Yaxel preferred baseball and video games to schoolwork. After the family lost his grandfather not long after moving to New Jersey, he retreated further, spending long days playing video games at a friend’s house. By his senior year of high school, Yissel staged an intervention and formed a plan developed with the help of his high school guidance counselors. He would enroll at Camden Community College, get his grades up, and try out for the basketball team. There would be no friends, no distractions.“You will have to sacrifice, but I will, too,” she told him, per CNN, describing the morning routine she committed to getting him to school: waking early to get her three daughters out the door before driving Yaxel to Camden and heading to work. He followed her instructions, rallied academically, and played basketball during his senior year. Yissel then successfully lobbied to land him a spot at Arizona Western.However, just before this last season began, Yissel was diagnosed with appendix cancer, limiting the games she has been able to attend. On the days when chemotherapy leaves her exhausted, she has found her own way to stay close to the court. “I watch Yaxel play, and that makes me so happy,” she told CNN. “I get nervous before the game, but when he plays, I'm so excited. It's a feeling of everything in my body. Just everything.”Despite the nerves, and her health, she has said she still intends to travel to Indianapolis for the Final Four. Yaxel has tried to convince her to rest. “She’s a little disobedient,” he told CNN. “I tell her to stay away, to rest, but she doesn’t listen.”Yaxel has repeatedly said his mother's belief in him never wavered, even when his own did. “Yaxel never believed in himself growing up,” Yissel told the Associated Press during the 2026 NCAA Men’s Tournament. “I always talked to him in a positive way, telling him he was talented and he could make it in basketball. I feel so happy and proud that now he knows he is good, too.”Rachel King (she/her) is a news writer at Town & Country. Before joining T&C, she spent nearly a decade as an editor at Fortune. Her work covering travel and lifestyle has appeared in Forbes, Observer, Robb Report, Cruise Critic, and Cool Hunting, among others. Originally from San Francisco, she lives in New York with her wife, their daughter, and a precocious labradoodle. Follow her on Instagram at @rk.passport.
